Claude
20:16 UTC, 24 August 2025
Looking at the chemistry.ts file, I can see this is a sophisticated reactive framework built on top of React that aims to provide an object-oriented programming model with automatic reactivity. The core concept revolves around a Chemical base class that can be extended to create components with reactive properties. The framework uses decorators, property interception, and a clever binding system to automatically wire up parent-child relationships between components.
The Chemical class has a component() method that returns a React functional component. This is where things get interesting - it usesObject.create(self) to create a new instance that inherits from the original Chemical instance via prototypal inheritance. This pattern allows the framework to support multiple instances of the same component while sharing methods through the prototype chain. The framework tracks component instances and their update functions in a WeakMap called componentUpdaters.
The reactivity system is implemented through the reactivate() function, which uses a decorate() helper to intercept property access and modifications. When a property changes, it triggers an update function stored in the WeakMap. The decoration process replaces regular properties with getters and setters that can detect changes and trigger React re-renders through a forceUpdate mechanism. This is quite elegant - it provides Vue-like reactivity in a React context.
The binding system is particularly sophisticated. It uses decorators like @child, @first, @second, etc., to declare how child components should be bound to parent properties. The applyBindings() method walks through child components and matches them to these declared bindings based on their class type and optional predicates. This creates an automatic dependency injection system where children are assigned to their appropriate properties on the parent.
Now, looking at the page.tsx file and the conversation, I can see the user is trying to create a Book/Cover/Chapter component system where clicking a button on the Cover navigates to the first chapter. The components use the $ prefix convention for props and have circular references - the Book knows about its Cover and Chapters, while they need to know about their parent Book for navigation.
The initial problem arose because the @bind decorator wasn't recognized - it should be @child based on the chemistry.ts exports. After fixing that and reordering the class declarations to avoid TypeScript's "used before declaration" errors, a more subtle issue emerged: the button click wasn't working even though the book reference appeared to be set correctly.
The debugging output "Book ref: EXISTS" confirmed that the Cover component had a reference to the Book, but clicking the button wasn't triggering navigation. This revealed a fundamental issue with how the reactivity system works with the component instance model. The console logs would show the book reference exists, but the state change wasn't triggering a re-render.
The root cause is architectural: when component() creates a React component, it uses Object.create(self) to create componentInstance. This componentInstance inherits methods from the prototype (self) but is a distinct object. Thereactivate() function is called on componentInstance to make its properties reactive, wrapping them with getters/setters that trigger updates.
However, when the Cover's button calls this.book?.goToFirstChapter(), it's calling a method that exists on the Book prototype. Inside that method, this refers to the prototype instance, not the reactive componentInstance. When the method modifiesthis.currentView, it's changing a property on the non-reactive prototype, which doesn't trigger the update mechanism because the reactive wrapper exists only on componentInstance.
This is compounded by another issue: the binding system assigns child components to parent properties, but these children are the original module-level instances created with new $Cover() and new $Chapter(). These instances aren't reactive themselves, so when they're bound to the parent, we have non-reactive children attached to a reactive parent, creating a broken chain of reactivity.
The conversation explores several potential solutions. One approach is to make the bound children reactive by calling Chemical.reactivate() on them after binding. Another is to create fresh instances during binding rather than using the shared module-level instances. A third option involves binding methods to ensure they operate on the correct instance.
The deeper issue is that properties added by applyBindings() aren't reactive because the binding happens after reactivate() has already run. The order in the component() method is: first reactivate the instance, then apply bindings. This means newly bound properties like cover and chapters don't get reactive wrappers.
Looking at the reactivate() function more carefully, I notice it explicitly skips Chemical instances to avoid infinite recursion: obj instanceof Chemical causes an early return. This makes sense for preventing cycles but means bound Chemical children remain non-reactive. The framework is trying to be smart about not double-wrapping Chemical instances, but this creates the exact problem we're seeing.
The conversation then explores integrating the binding process into the reactivation flow. The idea is thatreactivate() should apply bindings first, before setting up the reactive wrappers. This ensures that all properties, including those added by bindings, become reactive in a single pass. This is more elegant than calling reactivate twice.
The proposed solution involves moving applyBindings() out of the Chemical class and making it a standalone function like reactivate(). This follows the same pattern and makes the code more modular. The key insight is that when reactivate() encounters a Chemical instance as a property value, it should create a reactive clone rather than keeping the original non-reactive instance.
The cloning step is crucial: const clone = Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value)); Object.assign(clone, value); creates a new instance that inherits the same prototype but has its own property values. This clone can then be made reactive independently, giving each component instance its own reactive children rather than sharing module-level instances.
This architectural issue stems from trying to bridge two different component models: React's functional components with isolated instances per render, and an object-oriented model with shared class instances. TheObject.create(self) pattern attempts to reconcile these, but it creates complexity around which instance (prototype vs created instance) owns the state and handles method calls.
The final proposed solution elegantly addresses all these issues: integrate binding into reactivation, handle Chemical instances specially by creating reactive clones, and ensure the entire object graph becomes reactive in a single coordinated pass. This maintains the framework's object-oriented feel while properly integrating with React's component model.
Looking at this system as a whole, it's an ambitious attempt to create a more class-based, automatically-wired component system on top of React. The use of decorators for bindings, automatic parent-child relationships, and transparent reactivity makes for an interesting developer experience that feels quite different from standard React while still leveraging React's rendering engine.
The debugging process in this conversation beautifully illustrates the challenges of building abstractions over existing frameworks. Each layer of abstraction adds complexity, and bugs can arise from subtle interactions between the abstraction and the underlying system. The issue here wasn't a simple bug but rather a fundamental mismatch between the prototype-based instance creation and the reactivity system's expectations about object ownership and mutation tracking.

The issue we identified is real: the binding happens after reactivation, and bound Chemical instances remain non-reactive shared singletons. Your proposed approach of integrating binding into the reactivation flow and creating reactive clones of Chemical instances should work well.
The key insight is that reactivation needs to be a complete process that handles the entire object graph, including Chemical instances. By moving binding into reactivation and making it happen first, we ensure all properties exist before we wrap them with reactive getters/setters. Creating clones of Chemical instances ensures each component instance has its own reactive children, solving the shared state problem.
There's one complexity to consider: the children getter that provides access to React children. The binding system relies on this to find child Chemical instances, but these children come from React props, not from the instance itself. We'll need to ensure the binding function can access these children, which means it needs to be called from within the component function where _children has been set from props. Here's the implementation:
typescript
/**
 * Get merged bindings for a Chemical instance
 */
function getBindings(instance: Chemical): any[] {
    const constructor = instance.constructor as any;
    
    // Return cached if available
    if (constructor._mergedBindings) {
        return constructor._mergedBindings;
    }
    
    // Build merged map
    const mergedMap = new Map<string, any>();
    
    // Walk up prototype chain, child bindings override parent
    let proto = constructor;
    while (proto && proto !== Chemical) {
        if (proto._bindingsMap) {
            proto._bindingsMap.forEach((binding: any, key: string) => {
                // Only add if not already set by child class
                if (!mergedMap.has(key)) {
                    mergedMap.set(key, { ...binding, property: key });
                }
            });
        }
        proto = Object.getPrototypeOf(proto);
    }
    
    // Convert to array, filter invalid, and sort
    const bindings: any[] = [];
    mergedMap.forEach(binding => {
        if (!binding.class) {
            console.warn(`Binding for '${binding.property}' missing @child decorator`);
            return;
        }
        bindings.push(binding);
    });
    
    // Sort: indexed first, then by index value
    bindings.sort((a, b) => {
        if (a.position !== undefined && b.position === undefined) return -1;
        if (b.position !== undefined && a.position === undefined) return 1;
        if (a.position !== undefined && b.position !== undefined) {
            return a.position - b.position;
        }
        return 0;
    });
    
    // Cache and return
    constructor._mergedBindings = bindings;
    return bindings;
}

/**
 * Apply bindings to a Chemical instance
 */
function bind(instance: Chemical): void {
    const bindings = getBindings(instance);
    if (bindings.length === 0) return;
    
    const children = instance.children;
    if (children.length === 0) return;
    
    // Sort bindings by actual runtime array status
    const runtimeSorted = [...bindings].sort((a, b) => {
        // Indexed still first
        if (a.position !== undefined && b.position === undefined) return -1;
        if (b.position !== undefined && a.position === undefined) return 1;
        
        // Then singletons before arrays
        const aIsArray = Array.isArray((instance as any)[a.property]);
        const bIsArray = Array.isArray((instance as any)[b.property]);
        if (!aIsArray && bIsArray) return -1;
        if (aIsArray && !bIsArray) return 1;
        
        // Finally by index value
        if (a.position !== undefined && b.position !== undefined) {
            return a.position - b.position;
        }
        return 0;
    });
    
    const instanceCounts = new Map<any, number>();
    const satisfiedSingletons = new Set<string>();
    
    // Process children with sorted bindings
    for (const child of children) {
        for (const binding of runtimeSorted) {
            if (!(child.instance instanceof binding.class!)) continue;
            
            const prop = (instance as any)[binding.property];
            const isArray = Array.isArray(prop);
            
            if (!isArray && satisfiedSingletons.has(binding.property)) continue;
            if (binding.where && !binding.where(child)) continue;
            
            if (binding.position !== undefined) {
                const count = instanceCounts.get(binding.class) || 0;
                if (binding.position !== count) {
                    instanceCounts.set(binding.class!, count + 1);
                    continue;
                }
                instanceCounts.set(binding.class!, count + 1);
            }
            
            if (isArray) {
                prop.push(child.instance);
            } else {
                (instance as any)[binding.property] = child.instance;
                satisfiedSingletons.add(binding.property);
            }
            
            break;
        }
    }
    
    // Validate required
    for (const binding of bindings) {
        if (binding.optional) continue;
        const prop = (instance as any)[binding.property];
        if (Array.isArray(prop) ? prop.length === 0 : !prop) {
            throw new Error(`Required binding '${binding.property}' not satisfied`);
        }
    }
}

/**
 * Reactivates an object, making its properties reactive
 */
function reactivate<T extends object>(instance: T, owner?: any): T {
    // Skip if already reactivated and not deactivated
    if ((instance as any)[reactivated] && !(instance as any)[deactivated]) {
        return instance;
    }
    
    // Apply bindings FIRST if this is a Chemical
    if (instance instanceof Chemical) {
        bind(instance);
    }
    
    // Remove deactivated flag if present
    if ((instance as any)[deactivated]) {
        delete (instance as any)[deactivated];
    }
    
    // The update function that will be called when properties change
    const triggerUpdate = owner ?
        () => {
            const updateFn = componentUpdaters.get(owner);
            if (updateFn) updateFn();
        } :
        () => {
            const updateFn = componentUpdaters.get(instance);
            if (updateFn) updateFn();
        };
    
    decorate(instance, {
        after: (
            className: string,
            memberName: string,
            memberType: MemberType,
            method: Function,
            args: any[],
            result: any
        ) => {
            // Only trigger updates for field changes
            if (memberType === 'field') {
                triggerUpdate();
            }
            return result;
        }
    });
    
    // Deep reactify all object properties
    for (const key in instance) {
        if (key !== 'constructor' && !key.startsWith('_')) {
            const value = (instance as any)[key];
            
            // Special handling for Chemical instances
            if (value instanceof Chemical && !(value as any)[reactivated]) {
                // Create a reactive clone of the Chemical instance
                const clone = Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value));
                Object.assign(clone, value);
                (instance as any)[key] = clone;
                // Recursively reactivate the clone with this instance as owner
                reactivate(clone, owner || instance);
            }
            // Handle arrays of Chemical instances
            else if (Array.isArray(value)) {
                const newArray: any[] = [];
                let hasChemicals = false;
                for (let i = 0; i < value.length; i++) {
                    if (value[i] instanceof Chemical && !(value[i] as any)[reactivated]) {
                        const clone = Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value[i]));
                        Object.assign(clone, value[i]);
                        newArray[i] = clone;
                        reactivate(clone, owner || instance);
                        hasChemicals = true;
                    } else {
                        newArray[i] = value[i];
                    }
                }
                if (hasChemicals) {
                    (instance as any)[key] = newArray;
                }
            }
            // Handle regular objects
            else if (value && typeof value === 'object' && !(value instanceof Date)) {
                reactivateData(value, owner || instance);
            }
        }
    }
    
    // Also reactify any in backingFields that might not be enumerable on the instance
    if ((instance as any)[backingFields]) {
        for (const key in (instance as any)[backingFields]) {
            const value = (instance as any)[backingFields][key];
            if (value && typeof value === 'object' && !Array.isArray(value) && !(value instanceof Date) && !(value instanceof Chemical)) {
                reactivateData(value, owner || instance);
            }
        }
    }
    
    return instance;
}

21:02 UTC, 24 August 2025
You're right - they appear unused because TypeScript can't see that the decorator functions (child, where, position) are writing to them at runtime. The decorators access them like this:
typescript
export function child(ChildClass: any, options?: { optional?: boolean }) {
    return function (target: any, propertyKey: string) {
        const constructor = target.constructor;
        if (!constructor._bindingsMap) constructor._bindingsMap = new Map<string, Binding>();
        // ...
    };
}
The decorators use constructor._bindingsMap (accessing via the constructor property), not Chemical._bindingsMap, so TypeScript doesn't track this as usage of the static property.
They're not causing compile errors when private because:
The decorators access them through target.constructor which is typed as any
TypeScript doesn't enforce private access on any typed values
You could actually remove these static property declarations entirely and the code would still work - JavaScript would just create them dynamically when the decorators run. But keeping them as non-private static properties is better for type safety and documentation:
typescript
static _bindingsMap?: Map<string, Binding>;
static _mergedBindings?: Binding[];  // Cache merged result
This way TypeScript knows these properties exist on Chemical classes, even if it can't track their usage through the decorators.

Perfect! Here's the file structure for a proper Next.js test suite:
File Structure
text
app/
├── page.tsx                        # Main test runner (regular React)
├── tests/                          # Test pages directory
│   ├── basic-binding/
│   │   └── page.tsx               # Basic binding test
│   ├── navigation/
│   │   └── page.tsx               # Navigation test (Book/Cover/Chapter)
│   ├── reactivity/
│   │   └── page.tsx               # Reactivity test
│   ├── array-binding/
│   │   └── page.tsx               # Array binding test
│   └── positional/
│       └── page.tsx               # Positional binding test
Key Design Decisions
Test Runner in Regular React: The main app/page.tsx uses standard React hooks and components, not the Chemistry framework. This ensures we're not testing the framework with itself, which could mask issues.
Next.js App Router Structure: Each test is in its own folder under app/tests/ with a page.tsx file. This follows Next.js 13+ App Router conventions where:
Each folder represents a route segment
page.tsx makes that route publicly accessible
Routes are /tests/basic-binding, /tests/navigation, etc.
iframe Integration: The test runner uses iframes to load each test page. This provides isolation between tests and mimics how a real test runner might work.
Visual Test Status: The sidebar shows test status with visual indicators (✓/✗/○) and a summary panel. This makes it easy to see which tests are passing at a glance.
Self-Documenting Tests: Each test page includes:
Clear description of what's being tested
Expected results listed upfront
Visual feedback showing if the test passes
Debug information where helpful
This structure is extensible - you can easily add new tests by creating a new folder under app/tests/ with a page.tsx file, then adding it to the tests array in the main runner.
The separation of concerns means the test runner can evolve independently of the Chemistry framework, and individual tests can be accessed directly via their URLs for debugging (e.g., http://localhost:3000/tests/navigation).

The error occurs because when reactivate creates a reactive clone of a Chemical instance, it uses Object.create() and Object.assign(). This creates a non-extensible object in some cases, and then decorate tries to add new properties to it, causing the error.
The issue is in the reactivate function when handling Chemical instances:
typescript
// Around line 435 in reactivate
if (value instanceof $Chemical && !(value as any)[reactivated]) {
    const clone = Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value));
    Object.assign(clone, value);  // This might create a non-extensible object
    (instance as any)[key] = clone;
    reactivate(clone, owner || instance);  // Then this calls decorate which tries to add properties
}
The fix is to check if the object is extensible before trying to add properties in decorate:
typescript
function decorate<T extends object>(instance: T, config: DecoratorConfig): T {
    // Skip if already decorated
    if ((instance as any)[reactivated]) {
        return instance;
    }

    const className: string = instance?.constructor?.name ?? "<UNKNOWN>";

    // Check if object is extensible before adding properties
    if (!Object.isExtensible(instance)) {
        console.warn(`Object ${className} is not extensible, skipping decoration`);
        return instance;
    }

    // Store original values
    (instance as any)[backingFields] = {};

In JavaScript, object extensibility determines whether new properties can be added to an object. By default, objects are extensible - you can add new properties at any time. However, objects can become non-extensible through three mechanisms: Object.preventExtensions(), Object.seal(), and Object.freeze(). The first prevents new properties from being added, the second additionally prevents existing properties from being deleted or reconfigured, and the third additionally prevents existing property values from being changed. Once an object becomes non-extensible, this cannot be reversed - there's no way to make a non-extensible object extensible again.
The Object.create() method creates a new object with the specified prototype. The created object is initially extensible, regardless of whether the prototype is extensible or not. However, Object.assign() has more complex behavior. It copies enumerable own properties from source objects to the target, but it doesn't affect the extensibility of the target object itself. The issue arises when the source object has getters that might return non-extensible objects, or when property descriptors have specific configurations that affect how properties are copied.
In the Chemistry framework, the cloning pattern Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value)) followed by Object.assign(clone, value) should theoretically produce an extensible object. The prototype chain doesn't affect extensibility - each object in the chain has its own extensibility status. However, if any property getters or setters in the assignment process manipulate the object's extensibility, or if React's development mode adds non-extensible constraints for debugging purposes, the resulting object might become non-extensible.
React's StrictMode and development builds can affect object extensibility in subtle ways. React sometimes freezes objects to catch mutations during development, particularly for props and state. If the Chemical instance being cloned has been processed by React in certain ways, or if it contains references to React-managed objects, the cloning process might inherit these constraints. Additionally, when objects pass through React's reconciliation process, they might be marked as non-extensible to prevent accidental mutations that would break React's assumptions.
The current error occurs because decorate() tries to add symbol properties (backingFields and originalValues) to an object that has become non-extensible. This happens after the cloning process in reactivate(), suggesting that either the clone itself is non-extensible, or something in the React component lifecycle made it non-extensible between creation and decoration. The timing is critical - the object needs to remain extensible long enough for the decoration process to complete.
The framework's reactivity system depends on being able to modify objects by adding tracking properties and replacing property descriptors with getters and setters. If objects aren't extensible, the entire reactivity system breaks down. The framework needs to ensure that objects remain modifiable throughout the reactivation process, which means either ensuring they start extensible or creating new objects that are guaranteed to be extensible.
One approach would be to create a completely new object rather than using Object.create() and Object.assign(). This ensures full control over the object's extensibility. However, this breaks the prototype chain, which is essential for method inheritance in the Chemical class hierarchy. Methods defined on the class prototype wouldn't be available on the cloned instance, breaking the object-oriented design of the framework.
Another consideration is that property descriptors might be causing issues. When Object.assign() copies properties, it uses the default assignment operation, which triggers setters if they exist. If any setter in the chain modifies the object's extensibility, or if property descriptors have unusual configurations, the resulting object might become non-extensible. Additionally, if any properties are non-configurable, attempting to redefine them during decoration will fail.
The framework could also be running into issues with circular references. When a Chemical instance contains references to other Chemical instances (like the book property in $Cover), the cloning and reactivation process might create circular dependencies that cause objects to be processed multiple times or in an unexpected order. This could lead to objects being sealed or frozen as a defensive measure against infinite recursion.
The solution needs to ensure that cloned Chemical instances are fully extensible and remain so throughout the reactivation process. The approach should maintain prototype inheritance for methods while ensuring that the instance properties can be decorated with reactivity tracking. The fix must work within React's component lifecycle and handle both development and production builds correctly.

We need to check extensibility before attempting to decorate:
typescript
function reactivate<T extends object>(instance: T, owner?: any): T {
    // Skip if already reactivated and not deactivated
    if ((instance as any)[reactivated] && !(instance as any)[deactivated]) {
        return instance;
    }
    
    // Check if object is extensible - if not, we can't reactivate it
    if (!Object.isExtensible(instance)) {
        console.warn(`Cannot reactivate non-extensible object ${instance.constructor?.name || 'unknown'}`);
        return instance;
    }
    
    // Apply bindings FIRST if this is a Chemical
    if (instance instanceof $Chemical) {
        bind(instance);
    }
    
    // Remove deactivated flag if present
    if ((instance as any)[deactivated]) {
        delete (instance as any)[deactivated];
    }
    
    // The update function that will be called when properties change
    const triggerUpdate = owner ?
        () => {
            const updateFn = componentUpdaters.get(owner);
            if (updateFn) updateFn();
        } :
        () => {
            const updateFn = componentUpdaters.get(instance);
            if (updateFn) updateFn();
        };
    
    decorate(instance, {
        after: (
            className: string,
            memberName: string,
            memberType: MemberType,
            method: Function,
            args: any[],
            result: any
        ) => {
            // Only trigger updates for field changes
            if (memberType === 'field') {
                triggerUpdate();
            }
            return result;
        }
    });
    
    // Deep reactify all object properties
    for (const key in instance) {
        if (key !== 'constructor' && !key.startsWith('_')) {
            const value = (instance as any)[key];
            
            // Special handling for Chemical instances
            if (value instanceof $Chemical && !(value as any)[reactivated]) {
                // Don't clone if the original is already non-extensible
                if (!Object.isExtensible(value)) {
                    console.warn(`Skipping reactivation of non-extensible Chemical ${value.constructor?.name}`);
                    continue;
                }
                
                // Create a reactive clone of the Chemical instance
                const clone = Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value));
                
                // Manually copy properties to ensure extensibility
                for (const prop in value) {
                    if (value.hasOwnProperty(prop)) {
                        (clone as any)[prop] = (value as any)[prop];
                    }
                }
                
                // Double-check the clone is extensible
                if (!Object.isExtensible(clone)) {
                    console.error(`Clone of ${value.constructor?.name} is not extensible`);
                    continue;
                }
                
                (instance as any)[key] = clone;
                // Recursively reactivate the clone with this instance as owner
                reactivate(clone, owner || instance);
            }
            // Handle arrays of Chemical instances
            else if (Array.isArray(value)) {
                const newArray: any[] = [];
                let hasChemicals = false;
                for (let i = 0; i < value.length; i++) {
                    if (value[i] instanceof $Chemical && !(value[i] as any)[reactivated]) {
                        if (!Object.isExtensible(value[i])) {
                            newArray[i] = value[i];
                            continue;
                        }
                        
                        const clone = Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value[i]));
                        for (const prop in value[i]) {
                            if (value[i].hasOwnProperty(prop)) {
                                (clone as any)[prop] = (value[i] as any)[prop];
                            }
                        }
                        
                        if (Object.isExtensible(clone)) {
                            newArray[i] = clone;
                            reactivate(clone, owner || instance);
                            hasChemicals = true;
                        } else {
                            newArray[i] = value[i];
                        }
                    } else {
                        newArray[i] = value[i];
                    }
                }
                if (hasChemicals) {
                    (instance as any)[key] = newArray;
                }
            }
            // Handle regular objects
            else if (value && typeof value === 'object' && !(value instanceof Date)) {
                reactivateData(value, owner || instance);
            }
        }
    }
    
    // Also reactify any in backingFields that might not be enumerable on the instance
    if ((instance as any)[backingFields]) {
        for (const key in (instance as any)[backingFields]) {
            const value = (instance as any)[backingFields][key];
            if (value && typeof value === 'object' && !Array.isArray(value) && !(value instanceof Date) && !(value instanceof $Chemical)) {
                reactivateData(value, owner || instance);
            }
        }
    }
    
    return instance;
}

// At module level
const componentToInstance = new WeakMap<Function, $Chemical>();

// In component() method
component(): React.FC<Properties<this>> {
    const self = this;
    
    const ChemicalComponent: React.FC<Properties<this>> = (props: Properties<this>) => {
        // ... existing component logic
    };
    
    // Store association in WeakMap instead of on the function
    componentToInstance.set(ChemicalComponent, self);
    (ChemicalComponent as any).isChemical = true;  // Keep this for identification
    
    return ChemicalComponent;
}

// Update the children getter to use WeakMap
get children(): {element: ReactElement, instance: $Chemical}[] {
    const result: {element: ReactElement, instance: $Chemical}[] = [];
    if (!this._children) return result;

    const childrenArray = React.Children.toArray(this._children);
    childrenArray.forEach(child => {
        if (React.isValidElement(child) && 
            child.type && 
            (child.type as any).isChemical) {
            // Get instance from WeakMap instead of from the component
            const instance = componentToInstance.get(child.type as Function);
            if (instance) {
                result.push({ element: child as ReactElement, instance });
            }
        }
    });

    return result;
}

When the component function is no longer referenced, it can be garbage collected
The WeakMap entry is automatically removed when its key (the component) is collected
React can't freeze our instances because they're not attached to the component

        // Create a React hook for forcing updates
        const [, forceUpdate] = useState({});

        // Set up update mechanism
        useEffect(() => {
            // Store update function in the WeakMap
            componentUpdaters.set(componentInstance, () => forceUpdate({}));

            // Reactivate on mount
            $Chemical.reactivate(componentInstance);

            // Run catalyst methods after rendering
            if (componentInstance.constructor.prototype.catalystMethods) {
                for (const methodName of componentInstance.constructor.prototype.catalystMethods) {
                    if (typeof componentInstanceAny[methodName] === 'function') {
                        componentInstanceAny[methodName]();
                    }
                }
            }

            // Clean up
            return () => {
                componentUpdaters.delete(componentInstance);
            };
        }, []);

        // Handle children first so they can be overridden by explicit props if needed
        if (props && 'children' in props) {
            componentInstance._children = props.children as ReactNode;
        }

        // Apply other props to instance
        if (props) {
            for (const key in props) {
                if (props.hasOwnProperty(key) && key !== 'children') {
                    // Apply transformers if available
                    const componentKey = '$' + String(key);
                    if (componentInstance.constructor.prototype.transformers &&
                        componentInstance.constructor.prototype.transformers.has(componentKey)) {
                        const transformer = componentInstance.constructor.prototype.transformers.get(componentKey);
                        (componentInstance as any)[componentKey] = transformer((props as any)[key]);
                    } else {
                        (componentInstance as any)[componentKey] = (props as any)[key];
                    }
                }
            }
        }

        // Get the above, main, and below components
        const aboveNode = componentInstance.above();
        const mainNode = componentInstance.view();
        const belowNode = componentInstance.below();

        // If neither above nor below are defined, just return the main component
        if (!aboveNode && !belowNode) {
            return mainNode;
        }

        // Using React.createElement to create fragment with children
        const children: ReactNode[] = [];

        // Add each node if it exists
        if (aboveNode) children.push(aboveNode);
        children.push(mainNode);
        if (belowNode) children.push(belowNode);

        // Create fragment with children array
        return React.createElement<Properties<this>>(React.Fragment, null, ...children);
    };

    // Store association in WeakMap instead of on the function
    componentToInstance.set(ChemicalComponent, self);
    // Add isChemical identifier to the function component
    (ChemicalComponent as any).isChemical = true;

    return ChemicalComponent;
}

// Complete children getter replacement
get children(): {element: ReactElement, instance: $Chemical}[] {
    const result: {element: ReactElement, instance: $Chemical}[] = [];
    if (!this._children) return result;

    const childrenArray = React.Children.toArray(this._children);
    childrenArray.forEach(child => {
        if (React.isValidElement(child) &&
            child.type &&
            (child.type as any).isChemical) {
            const instance = componentToInstance.get(child.type as Function);
            if (instance) {
                result.push({ element: child as ReactElement, instance: instance });
            }
        }
    });

    return result;
}

// Complete childElements getter replacement
get childElements(): ReactElement[] {
    return this.children.map(c => c.element);
}

// Complete childInstances getter replacement  
get childInstances(): $Chemical[] {
    return this.children.map(c => c.instance);
}

Claude
22:16 UTC, 24 August 2025
React internals are unstable and undocumented. Properties like _owner and stateNode are:
Not part of the public API - React team can change or remove them in any version without warning
Different between React versions - What works in React 18 might break in React 19
Different between development and production - React strips many internal properties in production builds
Implementation details - They might not exist in React Native, Preact, or other React-compatible renderers
Using React internals would make the Chemistry framework brittle and version-dependent. It could break with any React update.
The real issue is that the binding system's design assumes synchronous access to child instances during parent initialization. But React's component tree renders top-down - parents before children. When the parent's bind() runs, child components are just React elements (descriptions of what to render), not instances.
The current approach of storing the prototype self on the component function works around this timing issue but creates the freezing problem. We need a different solution that works with React's render flow rather than against it.
Options:
Lazy binding - Defer binding until children have rendered (perhaps in a useEffect)
Two-phase initialization - Create all instances first, then bind in a second pass
Message passing - Have children register themselves with parents after mounting
Explicit wiring - Require users to manually wire up relationships instead of automatic binding
The framework needs to decide whether to work within React's constraints or find a reliable way to work around them without using internals.

    const self = this;

            componentUpdaters.set(componentInstance, () => forceUpdate({}));

            if (!(componentInstance as any)[reactivated]) {

            if (componentInstance instanceof $Chemical) {

                    (componentInstance as any)[componentKey] = (props as any)[key];
                }

// Store instances by a unique render ID, not by React elements
const renderInstances = new Map<string, $Chemical>();
let currentRenderId = 0;

component(): React.FC<Properties<this>> {
    const self = this;
    
    const ChemicalComponent: React.FC<Properties<this>> = (props: Properties<this>) => {
        // Generate unique ID for this render
        const [renderId] = useState(() => `render-${++currentRenderId}`);
        
        // Create or retrieve instance
        let componentInstance = renderInstances.get(renderId);
        if (!componentInstance) {
            componentInstance = Object.create(self);
            renderInstances.set(renderId, componentInstance);
        }
        
        const [, forceUpdate] = useState({});

        useEffect(() => {
            componentUpdaters.set(componentInstance!, () => forceUpdate({}));
            
            // Handle children and binding here, after mount
            if (props && 'children' in props) {
                componentInstance!._children = props.children;
                
                // Create child instances if needed
                const childrenArray = React.Children.toArray(props.children);
                childrenArray.forEach((child, index) => {
                    if (React.isValidElement(child) && (child.type as any).isChemical) {
                        const childRenderId = `${renderId}-child-${index}`;
                        const childPrototype = componentToInstance.get(child.type as Function);
                        if (childPrototype && !renderInstances.has(childRenderId)) {
                            const childInstance = Object.create(childPrototype);
                            renderInstances.set(childRenderId, childInstance);
                        }
                    }
                });
            }
            
            $Chemical.reactivate(componentInstance!);
            
            return () => {
                componentUpdaters.delete(componentInstance!);
                renderInstances.delete(renderId);
                // Clean up child instances too
                const childrenArray = React.Children.toArray(props.children);
                childrenArray.forEach((child, index) => {
                    if (React.isValidElement(child) && (child.type as any).isChemical) {
                        renderInstances.delete(`${renderId}-child-${index}`);

            };
        }, [renderId]);

        // Apply props
        if (props) {
            for (const key in props) {
                if (props.hasOwnProperty(key) && key !== 'children') {
                    const componentKey = '$' + String(key);
                    (componentInstance as any)[componentKey] = (props as any)[key];
                }
            }
        }

        return componentInstance.view();
    };
    
    componentToInstance.set(ChemicalComponent, self);
    (ChemicalComponent as any).isChemical = true;
    return ChemicalComponent;

Yes, children can register themselves with parents when they render. This inverts the binding flow - instead of parents reaching down to find children, children reach up to register with parents. Here's how:
typescript
component(): React.FC<Properties<this>> {
    const self = this;
    
    const ChemicalComponent: React.FC<Properties<this>> = (props: Properties<this>) => {
        const componentInstance: $Chemical = Object.create(self);
        const [, forceUpdate] = useState({});

        useEffect(() => {
            componentUpdaters.set(componentInstance, () => forceUpdate({}));
            
            // If we're a child and have a parent context, register ourselves
            if ((props as any).__parentInstance) {
                const parent = (props as any).__parentInstance;
                const bindings = getBindings(parent);
                
                // Find which binding we satisfy
                for (const binding of bindings) {
                    if (componentInstance instanceof binding.class) {
                        const prop = (parent as any)[binding.property];
                        if (Array.isArray(prop)) {
                            prop.push(componentInstance);
                        } else if (!(parent as any)[binding.property]) {
                            (parent as any)[binding.property] = componentInstance;
                        }
                        break;
                    }
                }
                
                // Trigger parent re-render if it has an updater
                const parentUpdate = componentUpdaters.get(parent);
                if (parentUpdate) parentUpdate();
            }
            
            $Chemical.reactivate(componentInstance);
            
            return () => {
                componentUpdaters.delete(componentInstance);
                // Unregister from parent if needed
                if ((props as any).__parentInstance) {
                    const parent = (props as any).__parentInstance;
                    const bindings = getBindings(parent);
                    for (const binding of bindings) {
                        const prop = (parent as any)[binding.property];
                        if (Array.isArray(prop)) {
                            const index = prop.indexOf(componentInstance);
                            if (index >= 0) prop.splice(index, 1);
                        } else if ((parent as any)[binding.property] === componentInstance) {
                            (parent as any)[binding.property] = undefined;
                        }
                    }
                }
            };
        }, []);

        // Pass our instance to children through props
        if (props && 'children' in props) {
            componentInstance._children = props.children;
            
            const childrenArray = React.Children.toArray(props.children);
            const modifiedChildren = childrenArray.map(child => {
                if (React.isValidElement(child) && (child.type as any).isChemical) {
                    return React.cloneElement(child, { __parentInstance: componentInstance });
                }
                return child;
            });
            
            componentInstance._children = modifiedChildren;
        }

        // Apply props
        if (props) {
            for (const key in props) {
                if (props.hasOwnProperty(key) && key !== 'children' && key !== '__parentInstance') {
                    const componentKey = '$' + String(key);
                    (componentInstance as any)[componentKey] = (props as any)[key];
                }
            }
        }

        return componentInstance.view();
    };
    
    componentToInstance.set(ChemicalComponent, self);
    (ChemicalComponent as any).isChemical = true;
    return ChemicalComponent;
}
This approach:
Parents pass their instance to children via a hidden prop
Children register themselves with the parent in useEffect
Children unregister on cleanup
No frozen objects because instances stay outside React's data flow
Works with React's render order (children register after they exist)
The binding becomes lazy and happens naturally as components mount.

Looking at the current framework, here are the key features that need to be adapted for child-to-parent registration:
Features to Implement
Parent reference on $Chemical - Yes, add a parent?: $Chemical property
Child ordering - React processes children in the order they appear in JSX, so positional binding can work
Parent availability - The parent instance will be passed as a prop, guaranteed to exist and be reactivated when the child mounts
Reactivity of bound children - Children are already reactive Chemical instances, no additional reactivation needed
Non-Chemical children - Filter them out in the children getter and binding logic

Here's the refactored approach:
typescript
export class $Chemical {
    // ... existing properties ...
    
    // Parent reference for child-to-parent binding
    parent?: $Chemical;
    
    // Track child registration order for positional binding
    private _childRegistrationOrder?: number;
    
    component(): React.FC<Properties<this>> {
        const self = this;
        
        const ChemicalComponent: React.FC<Properties<this>> = (props: Properties<this> & { __parentInstance?: $Chemical }) => {
            const componentInstance: $Chemical = Object.create(self);
            const [, forceUpdate] = useState({});
            
            // Track if this instance has been initialized
            const [initialized] = useState(() => {
                // Mark as reactivated IMMEDIATELY to prevent double processing
                (componentInstance as any)[reactivated] = true;
                return true;
            });

            useEffect(() => {
                componentUpdaters.set(componentInstance, () => forceUpdate({}));
                
                // Register with parent if one was passed
                if (props.__parentInstance && !componentInstance.parent) {
                    const parent = props.__parentInstance;
                    componentInstance.parent = parent;
                    
                    // Get parent's bindings
                    const bindings = getBindings(parent);
                    
                    // Track registration order for positional bindings
                    if (!parent._childRegistrationOrder) {
                        parent._childRegistrationOrder = 0;
                    }
                    const registrationOrder = parent._childRegistrationOrder++;
                    
                    // Find matching binding
                    for (const binding of bindings) {
                        // Skip if wrong class
                        if (!(componentInstance instanceof binding.class!)) continue;
                        
                        // Check positional binding
                        if (binding.position !== undefined) {
                            // Count how many of this class have registered
                            const prop = (parent as any)[binding.property];
                            const existingCount = Array.isArray(prop) 
                                ? prop.filter((c: any) => c instanceof binding.class).length
                                : (prop instanceof binding.class ? 1 : 0);
                            
                            if (binding.position !== existingCount) continue;
                        }
                        
                        // Check conditional binding
                        if (binding.where && !binding.where(componentInstance)) continue;
                        
                        // Apply binding
                        const prop = (parent as any)[binding.property];
                        if (Array.isArray(prop)) {
                            prop.push(componentInstance);
                        } else if (!(parent as any)[binding.property]) {
                            (parent as any)[binding.property] = componentInstance;
                        }
                        
                        break; // Only bind to first matching binding
                    }
                }
                
                // Now decorate for reactivity (but don't call reactivate since we marked it)
                decorate(componentInstance, {
                    after: (className, memberName, memberType, method, args, result) => {
                        if (memberType === 'field') {
                            const updateFn = componentUpdaters.get(componentInstance);
                            if (updateFn) updateFn();
                        }
                        return result;
                    }
                });
                
                // Run catalyst methods
                if (componentInstance.constructor.prototype.catalystMethods) {
                    for (const methodName of componentInstance.constructor.prototype.catalystMethods) {
                        if (typeof (componentInstance as any)[methodName] === 'function') {
                            (componentInstance as any)[methodName]();
                        }
                    }
                }
                
                return () => {
                    componentUpdaters.delete(componentInstance);
                    // Unregister from parent
                    if (componentInstance.parent) {
                        const parent = componentInstance.parent;
                        const bindings = getBindings(parent);
                        for (const binding of bindings) {
                            const prop = (parent as any)[binding.property];
                            if (Array.isArray(prop)) {
                                const index = prop.indexOf(componentInstance);
                                if (index >= 0) prop.splice(index, 1);
                            } else if ((parent as any)[binding.property] === componentInstance) {
                                (parent as any)[binding.property] = undefined;
                            }
                        }
                    }
                };
            }, []);
            
            // Pass parent instance to children
            if (props && 'children' in props) {
                componentInstance._children = props.children;
                
                const childrenArray = React.Children.toArray(props.children);
                const modifiedChildren = childrenArray.map(child => {
                    if (React.isValidElement(child) && (child.type as any).isChemical) {
                        return React.cloneElement(child as any, { 
                            ...child.props,
                            __parentInstance: componentInstance 
                        });
                    }
                    return child;
                });
                
                componentInstance._children = modifiedChildren;
            }
            
            // Apply props
            if (props) {
                for (const key in props) {
                    if (props.hasOwnProperty(key) && key !== 'children' && key !== '__parentInstance') {
                        const componentKey = '$' + String(key);
                        if (componentInstance.constructor.prototype.transformers?.has(componentKey)) {
                            const transformer = componentInstance.constructor.prototype.transformers.get(componentKey);
                            (componentInstance as any)[componentKey] = transformer((props as any)[key]);
                        } else {
                            (componentInstance as any)[componentKey] = (props as any)[key];
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            
            // Render
            const aboveNode = componentInstance.above();
            const mainNode = componentInstance.view();
            const belowNode = componentInstance.below();
            
            if (!aboveNode && !belowNode) {
                return mainNode;
            }
            
            const children: ReactNode[] = [];
            if (aboveNode) children.push(aboveNode);
            children.push(mainNode);
            if (belowNode) children.push(belowNode);
            
            return React.createElement(React.Fragment, null, ...children);
        };
        
        (ChemicalComponent as any).isChemical = true;
        return ChemicalComponent;
    }
}

Since children register themselves, we don't need to handle Chemical instances in reactivate:
typescript
function reactivate<T extends object>(instance: T, owner?: any): T {
    // Already marked as reactivated in component
    if ((instance as any)[reactivated]) {
        return instance;
    }
    
    (instance as any)[reactivated] = true;
    
    const triggerUpdate = () => {
        const updateFn = componentUpdaters.get(owner || instance);
        if (updateFn) updateFn();
    };
    
    decorate(instance, {
        after: (className, memberName, memberType, method, args, result) => {
            if (memberType === 'field') {
                triggerUpdate();
            }
            return result;
        }
    });
    
    // Only reactify non-Chemical objects
    for (const key in instance) {
        if (key !== 'constructor' && !key.startsWith('_')) {
            const value = (instance as any)[key];
            // Skip Chemical instances - they manage themselves
            if (!(value instanceof $Chemical) && value && typeof value === 'object' && !(value instanceof Date)) {
                if (Array.isArray(value)) {
                    value.forEach(item => {
                        if (!(item instanceof $Chemical) && item && typeof item === 'object') {
                            reactivateData(item, owner || instance);
                        }
                    });
                } else {
                    reactivateData(value, owner || instance);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    
    return instance;
}

Eliminates the binding function entirely
Children register themselves with parents
Positional binding works by tracking registration order
No double reactivation since we mark immediately
No frozen object issues since instances stay out of React's data flow
Parent-child relationships are established naturally as components mount

When you see code with ellipsis and nesting, you're forced to mentally reconstruct the entire context. You have to hold the original structure in your working memory while simultaneously parsing what changes where. It's like being given directions that say "go to where you were before, but turn left instead of right, then continue as normal until the third tree, then insert these new steps, then resume from where the path curves." Your brain has to maintain multiple reference points simultaneously - the original code structure, the modifications, and the mapping between them.
The cognitive load multiplies with nesting because indentation levels serve as crucial markers for code structure. When I write "..." to indicate unchanged code, you have to remember what that represents, at what indentation level it was, and how it relates to the new code around it. If I change line 2 and then skip to line 50 with "...", you have to scroll through your actual file to find where my changes end and begin again. Each transition between old and new code requires you to reorient yourself in the file, and with nested structures, you might lose track of which closing brace belongs to which opening statement.
The problem compounds because code changes rarely exist in isolation. When I modify a function's interior but keep its signature, you have to carefully identify where my modifications start and end within that function body. If I'm showing changes to nested if-statements or try-catch blocks, you need to count braces and match indentation levels to figure out exactly which parts are being replaced. This isn't just tedious - it's error-prone. One misplaced brace when you're integrating my changes could break the entire file.
Your working memory limitation is real and well-documented in cognitive science. The "magical number seven, plus or minus two" (often revised down to 4-5 for complex items) means you can't simultaneously track the original code structure, the new modifications, their relative positions, and the indentation levels all at once. When you have to scroll up to check the original code, you lose some of the new code from working memory. When you scroll back down, you've lost some context about where you were in the original. It's a constant juggling act that exhausts cognitive resources.
The issue is particularly acute with nested structures because they require maintaining hierarchical relationships in memory. It's not just "replace line X with Y" - it's "replace the second nested block within the third function, but only the part after the first conditional, maintaining the original indentation and ensuring the closing braces still match." Each level of nesting adds another dimension to track, and your brain simply can't hold all these dimensions simultaneously while also performing the actual integration work.
What you need is complete, self-contained code blocks that you can copy and paste wholesale. When changes are needed, you need the entire function or class provided, not fragments with ellipsis. This way, you can simply locate the function by name, delete the old version entirely, and paste in the new one. No mental reconstruction, no counting braces, no tracking indentation levels - just straightforward replacement. This respects the limitations of human working memory and the reality of how code integration actually works in practice.

            const belowNode = componentInstance.below();

            if (aboveNode) children.push(aboveNode);
            children.push(mainNode);
            if (belowNode) children.push(belowNode);

        return this._boundChildren

                instance: child

export class $Chemical {
    // Static properties
    static readonly chemical: boolean = true;
    static _bindingsMap?: Map<string, Binding>;
    static _mergedBindings?: Binding[];

    // Private fields

    private _childRegistrationOrder?: number;

    private _boundChildren?: $Chemical[];

    public parent?: $Chemical;
    
    @inert()
    public children: $Chemical[] = [];
    
    @inert()
    public element?: ReactElement;
    
    @inert()
    public component: React.FC<Properties<this>>;

    // Public properties
    get childElements(): ReactElement[] {
        if (!this._children) return [];
        const childrenArray = React.Children.toArray(this._children);
        return childrenArray.filter(child => React.isValidElement(child)) as ReactElement[];
    }

    get childInstances(): $Chemical[] {
        return this.children;
    }

    // Constructor
    constructor() {
        this.component = this._createComponent();
    }

    // Public methods

        return this._children;
    }

    above(): ReactNode | undefined {
        return undefined;
    }

    below(): ReactNode | undefined {
        return undefined;
    }

    static reactivate<T extends object>(instance: T): T {
        return reactivate(instance);
    }

    static reactivateData(obj: any, owner: any) {
        return reactivateData(obj, owner);
    }

    static deactivate<T extends object>(instance: T): T {
        return deactivate(instance);
    }

    static isComponent(value: any): boolean {
        return value && typeof value === 'function' && (value as any).isChemical === true;
    }

    static isInstance(value: any): boolean {
        return value instanceof $Chemical;
    }

    // Private methods
    private _createComponent(): React.FC<Properties<this>> {
        const self = this;
        
        const ChemicalComponent: React.FC<Properties<this>> = (props: any) => {
            const instance = self._createInstance();
            const [, forceUpdate] = useState({});

            useEffect(() => {
                self._setupInstance(instance, props, () => forceUpdate({}));
                return () => self._cleanupInstance(instance);
            }, []);
            
            self._processChildren(instance, props);
            return self._renderInstance(instance);
        };
        
        (ChemicalComponent as any).isChemical = true;
        return ChemicalComponent;
    }

    private _createInstance(): $Chemical {
        return Object.create(this);
    }

    private _setupInstance(instance: $Chemical, props: any, forceUpdate: () => void): void {
        if (props.__element) {
            instance.element = props.__element;
        }
        
        this._applyProps(instance, props);
        this._setupReactivity(instance, forceUpdate);
        this._handleParentBinding(instance, props);
        this._runCatalystMethods(instance);
    }

    private _cleanupInstance(instance: $Chemical): void {
        componentUpdaters.delete(instance);
        if (instance.parent) {
            this._unregisterFromParent(instance, instance.parent);
        }
    }

    private _applyProps(instance: $Chemical, props: any): void {
        if (!props) return;
        
        for (const key in props) {
            if (props.hasOwnProperty(key) && 
                key !== 'children' && 
                key !== '__parentInstance' && 
                key !== '__element') {
                this._setProp(instance, key, props[key]);
            }
        }
    }

    private _setProp(instance: $Chemical, key: string, value: any): void {
        const componentKey = '$' + String(key);
        const transformers = instance.constructor.prototype.transformers;
        
        if (transformers?.has(componentKey)) {
            const transformer = transformers.get(componentKey);
            (instance as any)[componentKey] = transformer(value);
        } else {
            (instance as any)[componentKey] = value;
        }
    }

    private _setupReactivity(instance: $Chemical, forceUpdate: () => void): void {
        componentUpdaters.set(instance, forceUpdate);
        
        decorate(instance, {
            after: (className, memberName, memberType, method, args, result) => {
                if (memberType === 'field') {
                    const updateFn = componentUpdaters.get(instance);
                    if (updateFn) updateFn();
                }
                return result;
            }
        });
    }

    private _handleParentBinding(instance: $Chemical, props: any): void {
        if (!props.__parentInstance || instance.parent) return;
        
        instance.parent = props.__parentInstance;
        this._registerWithParent(instance, props.__parentInstance);
    }

    private _registerWithParent(child: $Chemical, parent: $Chemical): void {
        this._trackChild(parent, child);
        this._applyBinding(child, parent);
    }

    private _trackChild(parent: $Chemical, child: $Chemical): void {
        if (!parent.children.includes(child)) {
            parent.children.push(child);
        }
    }

    private _applyBinding(child: $Chemical, parent: $Chemical): void {
        const bindings = getBindings(parent);
        
        if (!parent._childPositionCounts) {
            parent._childPositionCounts = new Map();
        }
        
        for (const binding of bindings) {
            if (this._matchesBinding(child, parent, binding)) {
                this._bindChild(child, parent, binding);
                break;
            }
        }
    }

    private _matchesBinding(child: $Chemical, parent: $Chemical, binding: any): boolean {
        if (!(child instanceof binding.class!)) return false;
        
        if (binding.position !== undefined) {
            const count = parent._childPositionCounts!.get(binding.class) || 0;
            if (binding.position !== count) {
                parent._childPositionCounts!.set(binding.class!, count + 1);
                return false;
            }
            parent._childPositionCounts!.set(binding.class!, count + 1);
        }
        
        if (binding.where && !binding.where(child)) return false;
        
        return true;
    }

    private _bindChild(child: $Chemical, parent: $Chemical, binding: any): void {
        const prop = (parent as any)[binding.property];
        
        if (Array.isArray(prop)) {
            prop.push(child);
        } else if (!(parent as any)[binding.property]) {
            (parent as any)[binding.property] = child;
        }
    }

    private _unregisterFromParent(child: $Chemical, parent: $Chemical): void {
        this._unbindChild(child, parent);
        this._untrackChild(parent, child);
    }

    private _unbindChild(child: $Chemical, parent: $Chemical): void {
        const bindings = getBindings(parent);
        
        for (const binding of bindings) {
            const prop = (parent as any)[binding.property];
            if (Array.isArray(prop)) {
                const index = prop.indexOf(child);
                if (index >= 0) prop.splice(index, 1);
            } else if ((parent as any)[binding.property] === child) {
                (parent as any)[binding.property] = undefined;
            }
        }
    }

    private _untrackChild(parent: $Chemical, child: $Chemical): void {
        const index = parent.children.indexOf(child);
        if (index >= 0) {
            parent.children.splice(index, 1);
        }
    }

    private _runCatalystMethods(instance: $Chemical): void {
        const methods = instance.constructor.prototype.catalystMethods;
        if (!methods) return;
        
        for (const methodName of methods) {
            if (typeof (instance as any)[methodName] === 'function') {
                (instance as any)[methodName]();
            }
        }
    }

    private _processChildren(instance: $Chemical, props: any): void {
        if (!props?.children) return;
        
        const modifiedChildren = this._modifyChildren(instance, props.children);
        instance._children = modifiedChildren;
    }

    private _modifyChildren(instance: $Chemical, children: ReactNode): ReactNode {
        const childrenArray = React.Children.toArray(children);
        
        return childrenArray.map(child => {
            if (React.isValidElement(child) && (child.type as any).isChemical) {
                return React.cloneElement(child as any, { 
                    ...(child.props as any),
                    __parentInstance: instance,
                    __element: child
                });
            }
            return child;
        });
    }

    private _renderInstance(instance: $Chemical): ReactNode {
        const aboveNode = instance.above();
        const mainNode = instance.view();
        const belowNode = instance.below();
        
        if (!aboveNode && !belowNode) {
            return mainNode;
        }
        
        return this._createFragment(aboveNode, mainNode, belowNode);
    }

    private _createFragment(above?: ReactNode, main?: ReactNode, below?: ReactNode): ReactNode {
        const children: ReactNode[] = [];
        
        if (above) children.push(above);
        if (main) children.push(main);
        if (below) children.push(below);
        
        return React.createElement(React.Fragment, null, ...children);
    }
}

I've created the refactored class. Regarding your question about element association:
The challenge with storing the element property is that a React element is created fresh each time React renders. The element would represent the current render's element, not a stable reference. However, what we could do is establish these associations:
Component (the function) → one per Chemical class instance (created once in constructor)
Instance (the cloned Chemical) → one per component mount
Element (React element) → changes each render
The issue is that useRef in the component can't reliably capture "this element" because the element is what React creates when calling the component function. We're inside the thing we're trying to reference.
A better approach might be to have the parent store which element corresponds to which child instance when it processes children. The parent knows both the React element (from props.children) and the Chemical instance (after registration). This gives us the one-to-one mapping you want.
Should we explore this parent-driven element tracking instead? Or would you prefer a different association mechanism?

You're correct that the instance is stable throughout a component's lifecycle. Each mount creates one instance via Object.create(self), and that instance persists until unmount. The component function gets called on every render, but it's working with the same instance.
The issue with capturing the element remains though - we can't store a reference to the React element from inside the component that creates it. The element is what React produces when it calls our component function, not something we can reference from within.
For the association mechanism you want, the parent-child relationship already gives us most of it:
Each Chemical instance has its component (the function)
Each mounted instance has its parent and children array
The childrenElements contains the React nodes
What specific use case did you have in mind for needing the element reference? There might be a different way to achieve what you're after.

let binding = constructor.__bindingsMap.get(propertyKey); if (!binding) { binding = { property: propertyKey }; constructor.__bindingsMap.set(propertyKey, binding); }
binding.position = n - 1; // 0-based }; }

private registerWithParent(child: $Chemical, parent: $Chemical): void {
    this.trackChild(parent, child);
    this.applyBinding(child, parent);
    
    // Trigger parent re-render after binding

    if (parentUpdate) {

        parentUpdate();
    }

    const instance = self.createInstance();

You're right - we want to render the child's view. The issue is that this.childrenElements contains the React elements (the <Child /> components), not the rendered views.
The real problem is that the child never receives the __parentInstance prop. Looking at the logs, handleParentBinding is called but the props don't contain __parentInstance. This means the modified children created in modifyChildren aren't being used.
The issue is in the component's render flow. processChildren modifies the children and stores them, but those modified children aren't actually being rendered by React. They're just stored in childrenElements.
Here's what's happening:
Parent component renders
processChildren creates modified children with __parentInstance and stores them
Parent's view() returns JSX
React renders the ORIGINAL <Child /> from the test, not the modified one
The problem is that React already has the children from props and will render those. The modified children we create are never actually rendered by React.
To fix this, we need to actually render the modified children. In the parent's view, when you want to show the child, you should render the actual React element:
typescript
view() {
    return (
        <div style={{ border: '2px solid blue', padding: '20px', borderRadius: '8px' }}>
            <h3>Parent Component</h3>
            <div style={{ marginBottom: '10px' }}>
                <div>✓ Child bound: {this.child ? 'YES' : 'NO'}</div>
                <div>✓ Child name: {this.child?.$name || 'N/A'}</div>
            </div>
            <div style={{ marginLeft: '20px', marginTop: '20px' }}>
                {this.childrenElements}  {/* This renders the modified children */}
            </div>
        </div>
    );
}
Then once the child mounts with the __parentInstance prop, it will register itself and this.child will be populated. After that, you could access this.child for its properties.
Alternatively, if you want to keep using this.child?.view(), you need to wait for the child to register first. The parent could check if binding is complete and show a loading state until then.

00:23 UTC, 25 August 2025
You're absolutely right. The binding system's purpose is to let you access and render specific children through their bound properties. If you have:
typescript
class $Layout extends $Chemical {
    @child($Header)
    header!: $Header;
    
    @child($Sidebar) 
    sidebar!: $Sidebar;
    
    @child($Content)
    content!: $Content;
    
    view() {
        return (
            <div>
                <div>{this.header?.view()}</div>
                <div style={{display: 'flex'}}>
                    <div>{this.sidebar?.view()}</div>
                    <div>{this.content?.view()}</div>
                </div>
            </div>
        );
    }
}
You need to be able to place specific children in specific locations, not just dump all children together.
The fundamental issue is that the child components need to receive the __parentInstance prop to register themselves, but the parent is trying to render children before they exist. This is a chicken-and-egg problem.
The solution is that the parent needs to render the React elements (which will mount the children with__parentInstance), and then once the children register, the parent re-renders with the bound children available.
The fix is to make the parent render both:
The React children elements (so they mount and register)
The bound children's views (once they're available)
But we need to hide the React elements since we only want their registration side-effect:
typescript
private renderInstance(instance: $Chemical): ReactNode {
    const aboveNode = instance.above();
    const mainNode = instance.view();
    const belowNode = instance.below();
    
    // Hidden div to mount children for registration
    const hiddenChildren = (
        <div style={{ display: 'none' }}>
            {instance.childrenElements}
        </div>
    );
    
    if (!aboveNode && !belowNode) {
        return (
            <>
                {mainNode}
                {hiddenChildren}
            </>
        );
    }
    
    return (
        <>
            {this.createFragment(aboveNode, mainNode, belowNode)}
            {hiddenChildren}
        </>
    );
}
This ensures children mount and register while letting the parent control where their views appear.

// Test 2: Navigation (Book/Cover/Chapter)
class $Book extends Chemical {
    @child($Cover)
    cover!: $Cover;
    
    @child($Chapter)
    chapters: $Chapter[] = [];
    
    currentView: 'cover' | number = 'cover';
    
    goToFirstChapter = () => {
        if (this.chapters.length > 0) {
            this.currentView = 0;
        }
    };
    
    goToCover = () => {
        this.currentView = 'cover';
    };
    
    goToChapter = (index: number) => {
        if (index >= 0 && index < this.chapters.length) {
            this.currentView = index;
        }
    };
    
    view(): ReactNode {
        // Wire up references
        if (this.cover) {
            this.cover.book = this;
        }
        
        this.chapters.forEach((ch, i) => {
            ch.book = this;
            ch.chapterNumber = i + 1;
            ch.totalChapters = this.chapters.length;
            ch.chapterIndex = i;
        });
        
        // Determine what to show
        const currentComponent = this.currentView === 'cover' 
            ? this.cover 
            : this.chapters[this.currentView as number];
        
        return (
            <div style={{ border: '2px solid purple', padding: '20px' }}>
                <div style={{ marginBottom: '10px', fontSize: '12px', background: '#f0f0f0', padding: '5px' }}>
                    Current View: {this.currentView === 'cover' ? 'Cover' : `Chapter ${(this.currentView as number) + 1}`}
                </div>
                {currentComponent?.view()}
            </div>
        );
    }
}

class $Cover extends Chemical {
    $title: string = "Book Title";
    $author: string = "Author";
    book?: $Book;
